title: Wood Mackenzie: four-hour battery storage now beats gas peaking on cost globally
gist: Wood Mackenzie's global LCOE update finds four-hour battery storage cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where both were modeled, with single-axis tracker solar the cheapest new build in 43 of 48 markets. Gas turbine shortages and fuel volatility push peaking costs up while Chinese manufacturing scale pulls storage costs down.

insights.claim: Four-hour battery storage is now cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where both technologies were modeled.
insights.speaker: Ahmed Jameel Abdullah
insights.so_what: Gas peaker economics are now worse than batteries everywhere modeled, undermining new peaking capacity build.
insights.quote: four-hour battery storage now less expensive than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where both technologies were modeled

insights.claim: Gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are raising peaking costs while expanding battery manufacturing keeps pushing storage costs down.
insights.speaker: Ahmed Jameel Abdullah
insights.so_what: Supply-chain tightness for turbines is a cost tailwind for storage versus gas.
insights.quote: Gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are driving up peaking costs
insights.locator: This economic shift is decisive and widening

insights.claim: Storage and solar together are redefining power system economics, closing off the case for new gas peaking capacity, with long-term contracted renewables increasingly setting the ceiling rather than the floor on power costs.
insights.speaker: Ahmed Jameel Abdullah
insights.so_what: Utilities and developers face stranded-asset risk in new peakers.
insights.quote: closing off the economic case for new gas peaking capacity
insights.locator: The structural shift we are tracking

insights.claim: Single-axis tracker solar is the lowest-cost new-build technology in 43 of 48 modeled markets, with onshore wind leading in five.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Solar is the default least-cost new generation across almost all markets.

themes.theme: Middle East, Africa and Asia Pacific

insights.claim: In the Middle East and Africa, single-axis solar is US$37/MWh, falling to US$24/MWh by 2035, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE are on track below US$20/MWh by 2033.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gulf solar costs set the global floor and enable cheap firmed power.
insights.locator: Renewable LCOEs across the Middle East and Africa

insights.claim: Four-hour storage in the Middle East and Africa costs US$120/MWh in 2026 and is forecast to fall 33% to US$80/MWh by 2035, displacing open-cycle gas on cost in every gas market in the region.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Regional power planning in the Gulf and Africa shifts toward storage over peakers.
insights.locator: Grid-scale battery storage costs are now decisively cheaper

insights.claim: China's grid-scale storage LCOE is more than 55% below the rest of Asia Pacific average of US$134/MWh, due to supply chain integration and scale, and competitive Chinese supply should pull the regional average to US$92/MWh by 2036.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Chinese manufacturing scale is the main global storage cost driver.
insights.locator: China leads the world on grid-scale storage costs

insights.claim: Japan, Australia and the Philippines will keep a storage cost premium because of import duties, high installation costs and domestic manufacturing policies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Trade and local-content policy preserve higher storage costs in some APAC markets.

insights.claim: Asia Pacific solar in the highest-cost market is more than 200% above the lowest in 2026, a gap expected to widen to 250% by 2030, while onshore wind costs vary more than six-fold across the region.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Regional cost dispersion implies uneven transition economics within APAC.
insights.locator: Utility-scale solar PV remains the most cost-competitive

themes.theme: Europe, North America and Latin America

insights.claim: Europe's turnkey battery capex rose about 2%, the first increase in three years, as cell prices rebounded about 10% from their 2025 low, with capex forecast to fall 12% by 2031 before lithium prices roughly double in 2029.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Battery cost declines may stall as lithium rebounds from oversupply.
insights.locator: Battery storage turnkey capex rose about 2%

insights.claim: Europe has the highest fossil-fuel generation costs of any modeled region, with levelized carbon costs projected to surpass fuel costs by 2030.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Carbon pricing will become the largest cost component of fossil power in Europe.
insights.locator: Europe carries the highest fossil-fuel generation costs

insights.claim: North American solar faces tariffs, anti-dumping duties and Section 232 restrictions, with module prices rising about 5% annually through 2030 for utility-scale, and 6% in 2027 and 14% in 2028 for residential and commercial.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: US trade policy is raising solar costs, particularly for distributed generation, while safe-harboured capacity cushions utility-scale.
insights.locator: Near-term solar costs are under pressure

insights.claim: US gas generation investment is entering a supply deficit cycle through the late 2030s driven by data centre load growth, keeping thermal capital costs elevated, while storage tax credits partly offset FEOC restrictions until a cost spike after ITC phase-out from 2038.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Data center demand is tightening gas supply chains and raising the relative appeal of storage and renewables.
insights.locator: Tax credits continue to provide a competitive advantage for storage

insights.claim: Latin America's single-axis solar is the cheapest source in 2026, with costs falling 38% by 2060, and onshore wind LCOE is forecast to fall nearly 21% by 2030 from US$73/MWh to US$58/MWh as Chinese OEMs intensify competition.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Chinese turbine OEM expansion is lowering wind costs in emerging markets.
insights.locator: Solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the lowest-cost
